query: High-entropy alloys can combine mechanical strength, wear resistance, corrosion protection, oxidation resistance, and thermal stability, while their large compositional space offers opportunities to tune degradation in harsh environments. Prior studies have largely considered wear and corrosion separately, and only a few reports address their combined action, leaving the governing behavior poorly understood. For a high-entropy alloy subjected to tribo-corrosion, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the coupled response and why? Describe a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, predict changes in total degradation and its wear and corrosion components relative to a matched baseline, state where the prediction should hold or fail, connect it to the available prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: During tribo-corrosion of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), frictional wear disrupts the initially protective passive oxide layer, exposing a fresh alloy surface that is more susceptible to localized corrosion. This corrosion, in turn, produces surface byproducts or roughening that accelerates subsequent wear, establishing a positive feedback loop that governs the coupled degradation response.
generation.material_initial_state: HEA that has developed a relatively stable passive oxide layer due to its inherent corrosion resistance.
generation.intervention: Subjecting the HEA to simultaneous sliding contact (tribological load) in an aggressive electrolytic environment (e.g., dilute H2SO4), alongside control tests with only mechanical wear or only corrosion exposure.
generation.conditions: Tests performed under controlled sliding conditions (e.g., in a pin-on-disk apparatus) within a corrosive medium under ambient or moderate elevated temperatures.
generation.structural_mediator: The protective passive oxide (or film) that initially forms on the HEA surface.
generation.mechanism: Sliding friction mechanically removes the passive oxide layer, exposing the underlying metal to the corrosive environment, which then accelerates localized corrosion. The corrosion products or changes in surface integrity further weaken the wear resistance, leading to enhanced material removal. This interdependent process creates a synergistic deterioration where wear and corrosion amplify each other.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to baseline conditions (wear-only or corrosion-only), the combined tribo-corrosion condition will result in a notably higher total degradation rate, with both wear volume and corrosion damage increasing. Although exact quantitative changes are uncertain, a non‐linear increase in degradation is expected due to the feedback loop between oxide removal (by wear) and subsequent corrosion acceleration.
generation.baseline: Equal-composition HEA samples tested separately under only mechanical wear (dry sliding) and only static corrosion (no sliding) conditions.
generation.boundary: This prediction should hold in systems where the HEA forms a sufficiently robust passive film under corrosion-only conditions. It may fail if the alloy’s oxide layer is inherently unstable or if wear conditions are too mild to cause significant oxide disruption.
generation.uncertainty: The magnitude of the synergistic effects and exact degradation rates depend on the specific environmental parameters (e.g., electrolyte concentration, sliding speed, load) and the intrinsic oxide film properties, so precise values cannot be specified without further experimental calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples: one set with the naturally formed passive oxide layer intact, and a second set where the oxide layer is deliberately removed (e.g., via a chemical etch) or conversely, pre-oxidized to enhance film stability. Subject both sets to identical tribo-corrosion testing in a corrosive electrolyte using a pin-on-disk setup under controlled load and sliding speed. Additionally, perform wear-only and corrosion-only tests as baselines.
measurements: Wear volume/profile changes using surface profilometry.
Electrochemical measurements (e.g., corrosion current density, potentiodynamic polarization curves).
Surface chemical analysis (e.g., XPS) to assess oxide film presence and composition before and after tests.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples with an enhanced or intact oxide layer do not exhibit a significant reduction in the synergistic degradation (i.e., similar or no lower wear and corrosion rates compared to samples with a disrupted oxide layer), then the hypothesis that oxide disruption governs the coupled tribo-corrosion response would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this study, bulk samples of a CrMoNbWV high-entropy alloy (HEA) were obtained for the first time by spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed (MA) powders at 1200 °C, 1300 °C, and 1400 °C. Microstructure evolution, phase formation as well as wear and corrosion behavior were investigated. The MA powders’ phase composition was found to be represented by body-centered-cubic (BCC) solid solution. The solid solution partially decomposed to Laves phases under the sintering, such as Cr 2 Nb and (Fe, Cr)Nb, and NbVO 4 -VO oxides mixture. The temperature increase to 1400 °C led to a grain coarsening of the BCC phase and decreased the Laves phase content accompanied by precipitation at the grain boundaries. The sintered samples showed high hardness and compressive strength (2700–2800 MPa) at room temperature. The wear tests demonstrated excellent results in comparison to conventional wear-resistant composites. The obtained samples also exhibited high corrosion resistance under electrochemical tests in H 2 SO 4 solution. The CrMoNbWV HEA has comparable mechanical and corrosive properties with the WNbMoTaV type HEA, but at the same time has a reduced density: CrMoNbWV—10.55 g/cm

Abstract The growing interest in refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) in the last decade is mainly due to their thermal stability, outstanding mechanical properties, and excellent corrosion resistance. However, currently HEAs are still not considered for use as common structural materials due to their inherent drawbacks in terms of processing and machining operations. The recent progress witnessed in additive manufacturing (AM) technologies has raised the option of producing complex components made of HEAs with minimal machining processes. So far, this could be achieved by using pre-alloyed powders of HEAs that were mainly produced by a conventional arc melting furnace (AMF) in the form of small compounds that were transformed into powder via a gas atomization process. To significantly reduce the production cost, the present study aims to analyze the ability to synthesize HEA WTaMoNbV via a laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) process using mixed elemental alloying powder as the raw material.
